title: Hidden Hazards: Conventional Fragranced vs Green Fragrance-Free Cleaning Product Testing
content: Cleaning products are a significant source of indoor volatile organic compounds (VOCs), particularly when fragranced. Although fragrance-free or “green” (FF/G) products are increasingly marketed as alternatives, limited data exist on their VOC emission profiles and potential health relevance. Fifteen cleaning products used in Canadian buildings were analyzed, including conventional fragranced (n = 11) and FF/G products (n = 4). Conventional products underwent modified micro-chamber analysis, while FF/G products were analyzed using bulk headspace sampling, followed by gas chromatography–mass spectrometry (GC-MS). The 35 most abundant tentatively identified VOCs per product were reported and evaluated using U.S. EPA, IARC, Health Canada, and NIH toxicological frameworks. Across products, 237 unique VOCs were detected, with concentrations ranging from 2 to >29,000 ng/mL. The most frequently detected compounds were d-limonene (80%), isopropyl alcohol (73%), ethanol (67%), and linalool (67%). Conventional products showed a higher prevalence of terpenes and esters, whereas FF/G products showed a profile characterized by alkanes and solvents. Each product emitted 1-8 potentially hazardous VOCs. Conventional products contained a wider range of potentially hazardous air pollutants, while green-labelled products also emitted 22 potentially harmful VOCs, including benzene, chloroform, and acetaldehyde. These findings suggest that product labels alone may not reliably predict VOC emissions. Improved ingredient transparency, emissions-based testing, and research examining real-world exposures may help inform strategies to improve indoor air quality and accessibility.
